summary: This is the Flask 1.1.x Quickstart documentation page, a tutorial-style introduction covering a minimal app, running the development server, debug mode, routing, static files, templates, request data, cookies, redirects and errors, responses, JSON APIs, and sessions. It includes code samples and explains key concepts such as context locals and url_for. The note is truncated before the end of the sessions section, and the page itself warns that it describes an old version (the latest stable release is 2.0.x).
one_line: Flask 1.1.x Quickstart guide covering a minimal app, routing, templates, request handling, responses, and sessions.
key_facts: The Flask 1.1.x Quickstart says it assumes the reader already has Flask installed.
The page warns that it is an old version and the latest stable version is 2.0.x.
A minimal Flask application imports the Flask class and creates an app with Flask(__name__).
The FLASK_APP environment variable is set to the module name (for example hello.py) before running flask run.
The development server started by flask run runs at http://127.0.0.1:5000/ by default.
Running flask run --host=0.0.0.0 makes the server listen on all public IPs, making it reachable from other computers on the network.
Enabling development mode via FLASK_ENV=development activates the debugger, the automatic reloader, and debug mode.
The page warns that the interactive debugger allows arbitrary code execution and must never be used on production machines.
Flask versions older than 0.11 did not have the flask command or python -m flask.
The route() decorator binds a function to a URL, and the converter types are string, int, float, path, and uuid.
The url_for() function builds URLs from a function name and keyword arguments for variable URL parts.
By default a route only answers GET requests, and the methods argument of route() enables other HTTP methods such as POST.
Flask configures the Jinja2 template engine automatically, and automatic escaping is enabled for templates such as .html files.
Flask stores uploaded files in request.files, and secure_filename() from Werkzeug should be used on client filenames because they can be forged.
Sessions are implemented on top of cookies and are cryptographically signed, so users can read but not modify them without the secret key.
